summary: Specifies a DHCP option, for both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, that carries civic location such as country, state, city and street address. It can describe the location of the client or of the DHCP server.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4776 defines DHCP options that carry a civic location, such as a country, city, street, or room. A client can receive the location in more than one language or writing system.

questions: what is a catype in dhcp
subtitle: DHCP options for passing a client or network location as structured civic-address fields.

tldr.problem: A device may need a human-readable location, but address structures differ between countries and may include more than a street address.
tldr.mechanism: A DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 option carries a location source, country code, and typed address elements. Repeated elements can represent the address in different languages or scripts.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4776 replaces RFC 4676 to correct the DHCPv6 option code. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 5774 and RFC 6848.

today: RFC 4776 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4676 and is updated by RFC 5774 and RFC 6848. It corrects the DHCPv6 option-code assignment from the earlier document.

sections.title: Why DHCP Can Carry a Civic Address
sections.content:
Some devices need to know their approximate location. The RFC gives IP telephony as an example: a device's location can help contact the appropriate emergency response agency and help responders find it.

This option carries civic information, such as administrative areas and street addresses. The RFC defines delivery from a DHCP server to a client, not location updates from a client to a server. If a network provides location through both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, both protocols must convey the same information.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP server can give a device civic location details such as its city and street. This RFC defines the server-to-client direction only.

sections.title: The DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 Options
sections.content:
DHCPv4 uses option code 99, named GEOCONF_CIVIC. DHCPv6 uses option code 36, named OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC. Both carry a what value, a two-letter country code, and civic-address elements.

The what value identifies whether the location refers to the DHCP server, a nearby network element, or the client. The RFC recommends using the client value when it is known. The DHCPv4 option has a minimum length of 3 octets; if it exceeds 255 octets, the long-options mechanism must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The option begins by identifying whose location it describes and which country it is in. The remaining elements carry parts of the civic address.

sections.title: Address Elements and Language
sections.content:
Each address element has a type, a length, and a value. Elements are optional and can appear in any order. Values use UTF-8, and abbreviations must not be used unless the element definition allows them.

The language element and script element identify how following address values are written; each remains in effect until replaced. The RFC defines defaults of i-default for language and Latn for script. A server should provide common renderings and must provide at least the rendering appropriate to the location.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address part carries a type that tells the client what the value means. Language and script markers let one option contain several readable forms of an address.

sections.title: Types of Civic Address Information
sections.content:
The civic address types cover administrative levels above the street, from national subdivisions through city divisions, neighborhoods, and groups of streets. Other types describe street directions and names, house numbers, buildings, units, floors, rooms, postal codes, and post office boxes.

Countries use different administrative structures, so the RFC gives examples of how the generic levels map to local divisions. All address elements are optional, allowing a server to send the fields it knows for a location.
sections.plainLanguage: The option can describe a place at several levels, from a region down to a room or seat. Each part has its own type so clients can interpret it consistently.

sections.title: Constructing a Postal Address
sections.content:
A recipient can assemble a postal address from the language-appropriate elements, but the result depends on country-specific rules. A post office box replaces street-address elements, while a postal community name replaces the civic community name.

The RFC does not define how to format a valid postal address. It also notes that a post office box alone is not a suitable location for emergency purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can use the address fields to form a postal address, but it needs country-specific rules to put them in the right order. A post office box is a mailing address, not a precise civic location.

sections.title: Example Address in Three Languages
sections.content: The RFC gives a symbolic example for Munich city hall in Germany. It lists shared address details and provides the state and city names in German, English, and Italian. Each language run begins with its language marker; the example uses the Latin script.
sections.plainLanguage: The example repeats address fields that change between languages and shares the fields that stay the same. This lets a client select a rendering suited to its reader.

sections.title: Protecting Location Information
sections.content:
DHCP messages provide no privacy protection, so someone monitoring the link between server and client can read the civic location. The RFC does not recommend this option on networks without access restrictions or network-layer or link-layer privacy.

To reduce exposure, a server should send the option only when the client requests it. Location should not be sent from a DHCP client to a server, because doing so implicitly grants the server broad retention and distribution permissions.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone able to monitor an unprotected DHCP link may read the location. Servers should send it only when requested and only on networks where that exposure is acceptable.
